blocks.text: The most important non-specific defence is provided by the germ-killer cell of the blood. They attack and kill the microbes. These cells patrol the bloodstream and wait for invaders. There are three basic kinds: macrophages, neutrophils, and natural killer cells.

Macrophages develop from monocytes (a type of white blood cells). A macrophage ingests a bacterium, by endocytosis, and kills it by its lysozyme enzymes. Some macrophages are fixed within some organs e.g., lungs, liver, spleen, and brain. But most of them patrol in the blood, lymph and interstitial fluid.

blocks.alt: A large pink macrophage with a ruffled surface and a long extension, surrounded by rod-shaped bacteria; one bacterium is being taken in at its edge.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.4: A macrophage attacking microbes (original drawing after the textbook's photograph, Figure 21.4).

blocks.text: Neutrophils are a type of white blood cells. They use three methods for killing pathogens. The first method is phagocytosis. In the second method, they release soluble anti-microbial chemicals on pathogens. In the third method, they generate and release network of DNA fibres. These fibres bind with pathogenic bacteria and kill them.

blocks.alt: One neutrophil at the top, with three arrows to its three methods: phagocytosis (a pathogen taken into a pocket of the cell), release of anti-microbial chemicals (granules released onto a pathogen), and generation of a network of fibres that trap a pathogen.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.5: Methods of neutrophils to kill pathogens (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.5).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Neutrophil, Pathogen, Anti-microbial chemicals, Fibres, Phagocytosis, Release of anti-microbial chemicals, Generation of network of fibres.

blocks.text: These are a type of T-lymphocytes and are also called cytotoxic T-cells. They do not kill invading microbes, rather they detect and attack the body cells that have been infected with viruses. They release special proteins, called perforins, which insert into the membrane of the target cell. It results in the formation of a pore in the membrane of target cell. This pore allows water to rush into the target cell, which then swells and bursts. They are also able to detect cancer cells, which they kill before the cancer cells have a chance to develop into a tumour.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says natural killer cells are a type of T-lymphocyte and are also called cytotoxic T cells. In fact NK cells are lymphocytes of the innate (non-specific) defence, not T cells, and they are not the same as cytotoxic T cells, which belong to the specific immune response (topic 21.3.2).

blocks.alt: A germ-killer cell of blood pressed against a target cell. A granule of perforins opens towards the target, perforins cross the narrow gap, and perforin rings form pores in the cell membrane of the target cell. The target cell's nucleus is below.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.6: Natural killer cell attacking an infected cell (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.6).

blocks.title: For Information
blocks.text: The patrolling cells (macrophages, neutrophils, and natural killer cells) do not attack their own body because all the normal cells of body contain a surface protein marker that identifies them. This protein is called self-protein. The germ-killer cells of blood do not attack the cells which have self-proteins. They only attack the cells that lacks such proteins.
